title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Problem of E740: among all space curves (x,y,z), find the one that makes ∫ w(v) ds a maximum or minimum, where v = √(x²+y²+z²) is the distance from a fixed point O, w is an arbitrary function of v, and ds is arc length. Euler sets up two second-order Euler–Lagrange equations. In the earlier sections he shows that every solution lies in a plane through O, z = my + nx. He then reduces the system to dφ = C dv / (v √(w²v² − C²)) (§41). The first integral w v t/√(1+t²) = C, with t = v dφ/dv, is w·v·sin(angle between curve and radius) = C. In modern terms this is the Clairaut/Bouguer invariant, or conservation of angular momentum.

This page:
(1) Completeness check. The two second-order equations require four arbitrary constants. Euler has them: m, n (the plane), C, and the additive constant of φ.
(2) §42 recovers Cartesian coordinates from the polar data (v, Φ) in the plane: x = δ v cos Φ, αy + βx = δ v sin Φ, z = my + nx, with α = (m²+1)/√(m²+n²+1), β = mn/√(m²+n²+1), δ = √((m²+1)/(m²+n²+1)). Check: the unit normal of the plane is (n, m, −1)/√(m²+n²+1). Choose orthonormal in-plane axes e1 = normalised projection of the x-axis, whose x-component is δ, and e2 = (0, 1, m)/√(1+m²). Then x = (r·e1)δ = δ v cos Φ, and r·e2 = ((1+m²)y + mnx)/√(1+m²) = (αy+βx)/δ = v sin Φ. So Φ is the true polar angle in the plane and the formulas are correct.
(3) Euler remarks that once planarity is known, one could put the reference plane AOB in the curve's plane. Then z = 0 and q = 0, and the problem reduces to the usual two-variable isoperimetric method. He says the long route was worthwhile for its artifices and because it revealed the property itself.
(4) §43 begins the observation, completed on the next page, that the integrand involves only v and ds. Hence the problem is intrinsically two-variable: find a plane curve about a centre with ∫ w(v) ds extremal. Section 44 then solves this in polar coordinates.

Modern reading: these are geodesics of the conformally flat, spherically symmetric metric w(r)²|dx|², or Fermat light rays in a radially stratified medium. Planarity follows from rotational symmetry, i.e. conservation of the angular-momentum vector.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page; the coordinate formulas I–III are verified to be correct.
Next page (§44): the printed or transcribed integrand ∫w√(∂x²+yy∂y²) should read xx∂y². The correct form ∂s = √(∂x²+xx∂y²) is given in the line just before, so this is a misprint.

deep.surprise_reason: The page completes a classical result: extremals of ∫w(r)ds are planar, with the Bouguer/Clairaut-type invariant w r sin ψ = C. It also contains standard coordinate bookkeeping and a methodological remark about symmetry reduction. All of this is well known, and the content is correct and routine.
transcription_corrections: Angle printed as Φ (capital-style phi) on this page, while the previous page uses φ; it is the same angle.
Transcription of this page is otherwise accurate.
On the next page the transcription 'yy∂y²' should be 'xx∂y²'.
